result: The study employed computational methods including Gaussian Network Model (GNM), Transfer Entropy (TE), and Anisotropic Normal Mode-Langevin Dynamics (ANM-LD) to investigate CFTR's allosteric communication network. These coarse-grained approaches were validated for parameter sensitivity and have been successfully applied to protein dynamics in prior work.
evaluation: All three reviewers accepted the computational methodology without criticism. Reviewer 1 noted the methods are 'generally solid,' Reviewer 2 found the approach 'particularly compelling' and appreciated that 'the authors updated the manuscript nicely to include the limitations of the chosen model (GNM),' and Reviewer 3 stated the 'modeling results are validated with experimental observations.'

result: GNM-TE analysis identified 60 residues as main allosteric sources in ATP-free CFTR, with 22 co-localizing with hinge residues (statistically significant). The computational predictions showed remarkable agreement with experimental observations, with mean 8 correct identifications versus 0.7 for random allocation (p=9×e⁻¹³), and many identified residues correspond to disease-causing mutations.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised this finding. Reviewer 1 stated the results are 'validated with available experimental observations,' Reviewer 2 found 'the TE of the Apo system and the corresponding statistical analysis particularly compelling,' and Reviewer 3 noted 'Key residues were identified as pivotal allosteric sources and transducers and may account for disease mutations.'

result: In the ATP-free state, dynamic fluctuations at ATP-binding sites facilitate initial nucleotide binding, with the dynamic infrastructure already present even when NBDs are separated. Entropy peaks are slightly shifted from ATP-binding residues to adjacent residues, and this shift disappears upon ATP binding when the entropy source role transfers to the ATP-binding residues themselves.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings about ATP-free dynamics without challenge. Reviewer 1 noted the 'results and analyses are generally solid,' and Reviewer 3 stated the findings 'are significant for understanding CFTR biology,' implicitly accepting the ATP-free state characterization as part of the overall allosteric mechanism.

result: ATP binding focuses diffuse dynamics that pre-existed in the ATP-free state, greatly rewiring allosteric connectivity. Upon phosphorylation and ATP binding, entropy peaks in NBDs match ATP-binding residues, gating and pore-lining residues assume dominant roles in allosteric signaling, and these effects are conserved between human and zebrafish CFTR.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the ATP-induced changes without criticism. Reviewer 2 appreciated 'the comprehensive discussion of a proposed mechanism by which allostery is achieved in the protein,' which encompasses these ATP-dependent transitions. Reviewer 1 confirmed the 'results and analyses are generally solid and validated with available experimental observations.'

result: Removal of the slowest GNM modes revealed additional allosteric clusters: a symmetric cluster in TMDs including gating residues and ivacaftor binding site, and a previously undiscovered asymmetric allosteric 'hotspot' in TMD1 near the R domain docking site that may explain why R domain deletion reduces channel opening events.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the discovery of the novel allosteric hotspot. Reviewer 1 stated the findings 'provide comprehensive insights into the allosteric mechanism,' and Reviewer 3 noted the results 'are significant for understanding CFTR biology,' which encompasses this novel discovery. No reviewer challenged the identification of this hotspot.

result: Despite structural similarity between NBDs, clear asymmetry exists in allosteric signaling: NBD2 (with catalytic Walker B glutamate) provides higher allosteric signaling and correlates more strongly with ECL1, while NBD1 shows tighter correlation with permeation pathway residues. In ATP-free CFTR, entropy sources are predominantly on NBDs, largely absent from TMDs except at intracellular loops 2 and 3.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the asymmetry findings without objection. Reviewer 1 noted the analysis 'characterized the role of disease-causing mutations' and found results 'generally solid,' while Reviewer 2 stated the discussion 'allows the reader to place the allosteric mechanism of this protein in the broader context of protein allostery,' implicitly accepting the NBD asymmetry as part of the mechanism.

result: After removing the two slowest modes in phosphorylated ATP-bound CFTR, entropy sources in NBDs migrate from ATP-binding sites toward intracellular loops (positioned to transmit signals to TMDs), while TMD allosteric peaks migrate toward the extracellular exit, preparing for ion exit.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these mode-removal findings. Reviewer 1 stated the 'findings provide comprehensive insights into the allosteric mechanism of this protein,' and Reviewer 3 confirmed the paper is 'well written and the results are significant,' accepting the hierarchical mode analysis without criticism.

result: ANM-LD simulations revealed the conformational transition pathway from ATP-free to ATP-bound CFTR (converging from 7.5 Å to 2.3 Å RMSD), showing global rigid body motions similar to canonical ABC exporters. Time-delayed cross-correlation analysis identified a cyclic allosteric signal propagation: NBD2 → ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, ECL1 → NBD1 → gating residues/permeation pathway → NBD2.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the ANM-LD trajectory and signal propagation pathway. Reviewer 1 noted the 'results and analyses are generally solid,' Reviewer 2 appreciated the 'comprehensive discussion of a proposed mechanism,' and Reviewer 3 stated the 'modeling results are validated with experimental observations,' all supporting acceptance of the conformational pathway findings.

result: GNM-TE analysis of drug binding sites revealed that type I correctors (lumacaftor/tezacaftor) bind at 'valleys' (non-allosteric sites) consistent with their folding-stabilization mechanism, while ivacaftor and elexacaftor bind at allosteric sources. Ivacaftor's binding site sends information to similar residues as ATP-binding sites (Pearson's r=0.83), demonstrating that ivacaftor potentiates conductance by mimicking ATP's allosteric signal rather than directly affecting gating residues.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the drug mechanism findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 stated the study 'characterized the role of disease-causing mutations' and found analyses 'generally solid,' while Reviewer 3 noted the results 'are significant for understanding CFTR biology,' which encompasses the drug mechanism insights. No reviewer questioned the ivacaftor mechanism interpretation.

result: The authors propose a mechanistic model integrating induced fit and conformational selection: R domain movement occurs by induced fit (phosphorylation as ligand), ATP binding involves conformational selection followed by induced fit for NBD closure, and transition to the conducting state occurs by dynamic allostery with rapid conformational sampling around the ATP-bound state.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the proposed mechanistic model. Reviewer 2 explicitly 'appreciated the comprehensive discussion of a proposed mechanism by which allostery is achieved in the protein' and noted it 'allows the reader to place the allosteric mechanism of this protein in the broader context of protein allostery.' Reviewer 1 found the 'findings provide comprehensive insights into the allosteric mechanism.'

result: The identified allosteric cleft in TMD1 near the R domain docking site is proposed as highly druggable and provides a new target for structure-guided screening of small molecules.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this therapeutic implication. Reviewer 3 stated the 'results are significant for understanding CFTR biology,' which would include therapeutic implications, and Reviewer 1 noted the study provides 'comprehensive insights,' accepting the druggability proposal without objection.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on CFTR biology, cystic fibrosis, ABC transporter family, CFTR structure and gating mechanism, allosteric theory (KNF, MWC, dynamic mechanisms), prior experimental evidence for CFTR allostery, FDA-approved CF drugs and their mechanisms, and limitations of the computational approach (R domain not included in simulations).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the background information and context without challenge. Reviewer 2 specifically 'appreciated the comprehensive discussion' and noted it provides proper context for protein allostery. Reviewer 1 found the manuscript presents 'useful analysis' with results 'validated with available experimental observations,' confirming acceptance of the background framework.
